next_steps: Unblock the four domains, or reassign. The exact ask, unchanged from Wave 33, is: for each object, the column list with types, nullability and defaults that the product code ALREADY selects, plus the file and line that selects it. That is a read-the-caller task, not a design task, and each domain can answer it from code it already owns.

The 7 objects and their owning domains: event_equipment, event_tasks, artist_licensing_deals, artist_license_templates (artist, 75 diagnostic hits); hiring_candidates (work, 4); pending_password_resets (qa, 14); error_reports (admin, 6).

If a domain cannot supply a contract, the correct outcome is NOT a migration. It is a decision to delete the product code that queries the object, because the Wave 33 evidence is that the repository holds no archived definition of any of the seven, so nothing was ever applied and nothing depends on them at the data layer. That decision belongs to the owning domain and to release, not to the database lane.

Do not let this sit behind a green gate. check:migration-chain, check:migration-validation and check:migration-ledger are all green right now and none of them knows these seven objects exist. The only artefacts that track them are the inventory and these handoffs.
blockers: The seven objects remain absent from both the active chain and lib/database.types.ts. Every tsc diagnostic they cause is still in the preserved Lint And Build log, and will still be there after any regeneration, because regeneration can only add what the chain creates.
The Wave 33 refusal to invent a column contract stands. Authoring a plausible-looking table to silence a type error is how a schema becomes a fiction that later code trusts.
